🐛 Bug
There is a linking error when linking libtorch_cuda.dylib.
To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

git clone https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch
cd pytorch
git checkout v1.6.0
git submodule sync
git submodule update --init --update ---remote --force
python3 setup.py bdist_wheel

🐛 Bug
We observed a big increase in inference latency after adding torch.inverse() in the code path. After investigation and comparison with moving the op to CPU we found that there is a huge difference in performance of that op on GPU vs CPU.
The matrix size in our case is 4x4 which small for the GPU but torch.inverse() should be using magma library which has heuristics to move the op to CPU. We didn't see any magma invocations as well.
Based on @ptrblck suggestion we tried inverse on batched matrix to see if that made any difference but that also didn't result in any improvement.
Performance Difference:
╰─ python torch_inverse_exp.py
GPU Time: 8.78560 ms
CPU Time: 0.07149 ms
cpu/gpu: 122.90x

We increased the matrix dimensions to 1024x1024 but even then GPU is slower than CPU:
╰─ python torch_inverse_exp.py
GPU Time: 17.25289 ms
CPU Time: 9.54982 ms
cpu/gpu: 1.81x

To Reproduce
Here is the snippet of code which can be run to reproduce the performance difference:
import torch
import time

a = torch.randn(4,4).cuda()
torch.cuda.synchronize()

num_iter = 100
def test1():
    s = time.time()
    for i in range(num_iter):
        x = torch.inverse(a)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    e = time.time()
    gpu_time = ((e - s)/num_iter)
    return  gpu_time

def test2():
    s = time.time()
    for i in range(num_iter):
        b = a.to('cpu')
        d = torch.inverse(b)
        y = d.to('cuda')
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    e = time.time()
    cpu_time = ((e - s)/num_iter)
    return  cpu_time

gpu_time = test1()
print("GPU Time: {:.5f} ms".format(gpu_time*1000))

cpu_time = test2()
print("CPU Time: {:.5f} ms".format( cpu_time*1000))

print("cpu/gpu: {:.2f}x ".format(gpu_time/cpu_time))

📚 Documentation
In our distributed docs under "Synchronous and asynchronous collective operations" we document work.wait() and work.is_completed(), but the documentation is not completely accurate in the case of NCCL.
For a NCCL Work object, wait() does not in general block the process and instead synchronizes the NCCL stream with the default stream. is_completed does check if the kernel execution is finished but can return false even after calling wait. It might also be useful to clarify the blocking behavior can be achieved with NCCL_BLOCKING_WAIT=1.

There has been a growing interest in orthogonal parameterization of neural networks, see, e.g., [1,2,3,4,5].
To use orthogonal parameterization with PyTorch one has to implement it themselves or use third party code.
It would be convenient if PyTorch has a built-in module nn.Orthogonalthat handles everything automatically.

Additional context

FastH is up to 20 times faster than the previous sequential algorithm (see image in bottom of page).

🚀 Feature
Export multi-layer LSTM/RNNs as ONNX scan op instead of creating multiple ONNX LSTM cells for multilayer torch.nn.LSTM.
Motivation
Enable efficient ONNX representations of RNN ops instead of generating graphs with single cell LSTMs.
Pitch
See "Encoding RNN using a Scan" in https://github.com/onnx/onnx/blob/master/docs/Operators.md#scan
Example
Sample LSTM export to ONNX (produces graph LSTM cells in torch v1.6.0)
import argparse
import os
import torch
from torch import nn

_EXPORT_MODULES = [
    # Module, Num Inputs, Input shapes
    (nn.LSTM(input_size=16, hidden_size=32, num_layers=2), 1, [(2, 16, 16)]), # input_0=[seq_len,batch,input_size]
]

def export_to_onnx(module, num_inputs, input_shapes, *, module_name=None, outdir=None, device="cuda"):
    """Export a module to ONNX
    Args:
        module: A quantized module
        num_inputs: An Integer of number of inputs to the module
        input_shapes: A list of tuple of integer indicates.
        module_name: String. Module name. Default None.
        outdir: String. Path to write ONNX file. Default None
        device: Default "cuda".
    """
    module.to(device)
    dummy_inputs = [torch.randn(input_shapes[i], device=device) for i in range(num_inputs)]
    if module_name is None:
        module_name = module.__class__.__name__
    onnx_path = F"{module_name}.onnx"
    if outdir is not None:
        onnx_path = os.path.join(outdir, onnx_path)
    input_names = [F"input_{i}" for i in range(num_inputs)]
    torch.onnx.export(module, tuple(dummy_inputs), onnx_path, verbose=True, opset_version=12,
                      input_names=input_names, output_names=["output"])
def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument('--outdir', default='', type=str, help="Path to write ONNX")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    for module, num_inputs, input_shapes in _EXPORT_MODULES:
        export_to_onnx(module, num_inputs, input_shapes, outdir=args.outdir)
if __name__ == '__main__':
    main()

As it says in the title, I found that the binomial sampler can occasionally return -1 (about 1 in a 100M trials). This is probably mostly a small issue, but it's a big issue if you're computing log probabilities from the output.
I created PR #38456 for this, which was then merged. Unfortunately the bug still appears which means that my fix was not relevant (I was not able to build pytorch at the time for testing, that's my bad!). I think that PR can remain merged as its harmless, but a fix for the bug is still needed.

I believe the bug is in [`binomial_inversion`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/aten/src/ATen/native/Distributions.h#L159-L177), specifically line 169. If the result of the standard uniform is very close to 1 (like, `> 0.9999999`) then `log(U)` evaluates to 0 and `geom_sum` doesn't increase for a round. The rate of this matches pretty closely with the rate I observe the bug, which is comforting because last time I had no friggin' idea why it was happening.

🐛 Bug
I launched a training of the DETR model on a server that automatically deletes all the files older than 30 days (which I hadn't realized before launching), which resulted in some unexpected behavior.
This is what happened, in order:

I extracted the COCO dataset.
I launched the training on 8 GPUs using torch.distributed.launch. I checked, it went well for 20-30 minutes.
Because the timestamps of the extracted COCO files are from 2017, the server's cron started to delete the files.
As a consequence, after about two hours, I got an error:

FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: '/data/coco/train2017/000000315242.jpg'

A few hours later, I checked the GPU usage, and surprisingly the training was still running on 7/8 GPUs (except on the GPU 6). I thought maybe there was some new "fault tolerance" feature recently added to torch.distributed.launch, so I went to check the checkpoints: none, and the std logs: none. The 7 GPUs were still at 100%. This is not good at all. The main process on GPU 0 was responsible for printing out the logs and saving the checkpoints, but it didn't do any of these despite running at 100%.

What I would like to have is that the training stops whenever there's an error (which is supposed to be the case, by default).
To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

Launch the training of DETR on COCO on multiple GPUs with torch.distributed.launch. (An alternative to DETR is the torchvision's official reference example on object detection.)
While the training is running, delete a bunch of training images.
Observe the results: some processes will obtain errors, some will continue to train (without saving anything).

Training should stop whenever there is an error.

🚀 Feature
Support additional arguments in nn.Identity.forward
i.e.
def forward(self, input: Tensor, *args, **kwargs) -> Tensor:
    return input
instead of
def forward(self, input: Tensor) -> Tensor:

🐛 Bug
torch.argmax() returning different indices to numpy.argmax() when the element values are the same.
To Reproduce
Code:
import torch
import numpy as np

arr1 = np.array([1,2,3])
arr2 = np.array([5,10,3])
my_list_arr = [arr1, arr2]
A = np.transpose(my_list_arr)
A

Output:
array([[ 1,  5],
       [ 2, 10],
       [ 3,  3]])

Code:
tsr1 = torch.tensor(np.array([1,2,3]))
tsr2 = torch.tensor(np.array([5,10,3]))
my_list_tsr = [tsr1, tsr2]
B = torch.stack(my_list_tsr, dim = 1)
B

Output:
tensor([[ 1,  5],
        [ 2, 10],
        [ 3,  3]])

Code:
np.argmax(A, axis = 1)

Output:
array([1, 1, 0])

Code:
torch.argmax(B, dim = 1)

tensor([1, 1, 1])

The returned indices should both be the same using numpy.argmax() or torch.argmax(), but the returned index for the 3rd element is different.

dlrm_jit = torch.jit.script(dlrm) sys.exit() # successful exit after compiling, no need to train

🐛 Bug
MultiheadAttention c++ API did not register parameters under some conditions. The most important ones are 'in_proj_weight' and 'in_proj_bias'.
Here is the parameter registration phase in c++ impl:

  
    
      pytorch/torch/csrc/api/src/nn/modules/activation.cpp
    
    
         Line 450
      in
      47766e6
    
  
  
    

        
          
           void MultiheadAttentionImpl::reset() { 
        
    
  


Here is the parameter registration phase in python impl:

  
    
      pytorch/torch/nn/modules/activation.py
    
    
         Line 842
      in
      75a4862
    
  
  
    

        
          
           def __init__(self, embed_dim, num_heads, dropout=0., bias=True, add_bias_kv=False, add_zero_attn=False, kdim=None, vdim=None): 
        
    
  


The problem here is that in python, the following code will register parameter automatically, but c++ version doesn't.
self.in_proj_bias = Parameter(torch.empty(3 * embed_dim))

The reason is that Module has a customized setattr which handles the parameter/module registration automatically:

  
    
      pytorch/torch/nn/modules/module.py
    
    
         Line 657
      in
      eace053
    
  
  
    

        
          
           def __setattr__(self, name: str, value: Union[Tensor, 'Module']) -> None: 
        
    
  


This will cause problem when people want to update parameters' value by iterating parameter that returned by calling parameters(), since some of the parameters won't be returned by c++ version. Here is an example:

  
    
      pytorch/test/test_nn.py
    
    
         Line 4678
      in
      f71cccc
    
  
  
    

        
          
           for idx, p in enumerate(model.parameters()): 
        
    
  


The possible equivalent c++ impl will be something like this:
torch::MultiheadAttention model(torch::MultiheadAttentionOptions(4, 2).dropout(0.0));
{
    torch::NoGradGuard guard;
    for (auto& p : model->parameters()) {
      auto sz = p.view(-1).size(0);
      p.copy_(torch::cos(torch::arange(0, sz, tensor_options).view(p.sizes())));
    }
}

Currently, c++ code will return two less parameters from module->parameters() than python version due to not registering the parameter correctly.

🐛 Bug
The check at 
  
    
      pytorch/cmake/Dependencies.cmake
    
    
         Line 958
      in
      0ec7ba4
    
  
  
    

        
          
           if(NOT ${pybind11_PREFER_third_party}) 
        
    
  

 has an issue: When the variable pybind11_PREFER_third_party is not set, it evaluates to empty leading to if(NOT) which cmake evaluates to "False" hence skipping the check
This means that during initial configuration one would need to define pybind11_PREFER_third_party to OFF which is impossible through setup.py.
Solution: Change the line to if(NOT pybind11_PREFER_third_party) which evaluates the variable correctly.
Note that the pattern if([NOT] ${variable}) is wrong in 99% of the cases: CMake evaluates the arguments to if already. This means that things like this fail:
set(BAR OFF)
set(FOO BAR)
if(${FOO})

Because CMake receives if(BAR), then evaluates BAR which is set to OFF and hence returns false
To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:

Install pybind11
python setup.py install

Expected behavior
System installed pybind11 is used

https://pytorch.org/blog/introduction-to-quantization-on-pytorch/
I got a pretty good speedup when running with a single thread. (This is a GRPC server application that serves pytorch models). However, I do not see any improvement when using multiple threads and processing multiple concurrent requests. This does not happen when dynamic quantization is not being used: I see pretty good scaling up to about 10 threads. cc #755
JAX and Tensorflow disagree about whether or not the grad of a complex tensor should be conjugated or not. Here is an easy way to see the difference:
from jax import grad

def f(z):
  return z * z

z = 0.1j

print(grad(f, holomorphic=True)(z))

gives 0.2j
However
>>> x = tf.Variable(0. + 0.j)
>>> sess.run(tf.gradients(x*x, x), feed_dict={x:0.1j})
[-0.20000000000000001j]

source: tensorflow/tensorflow#3348
PyTorch also has to decide which side of the field it will come down on. Right now on master it implements JAX. From reading the issue, here is my understanding of the pros and cons:
In favor of TF:

The gradient is the correct direction for doing gradient descent. This means you can use a "stock" optimizer (one that was written with only real parameters in mind) without any changes to the optimizer. In contrast, to do gradient descent with the JAX definition, you have to remember to conjugate first.

In favor of JAX:

When the TF definition is implemented directly in the gradient formulas (as opposed to doing a single post facto conjugation), you end up with ugly gradient formulas. For example, take a look at https://github.com/tensorflow/tensorflow/blob/70fd0a4436e3b49139653dc5b85d1c7df23f403d/tensorflow/python/ops/math_grad.py#L453 where TF has to explicitly conjugate the input. With the JAX style definition, you can mostly reuse your real gradient formulas.
The TF definition is less efficient, since you're doing extra conjugations in the gradient formulas. Even if you write the derivative formulas in the JAX way and then conjugate before plopping the gradient in x.grad, you lose the opportunity to do a fused conjugate-add for the optimizer update.

Gradient formulas look ugly seems like a clear reason to prefer JAX style. Posting this for other opinions.
cc @ezyang @gchanan @zou3519 @ssnl @albanD @gqchen @anjali411 @dylanbespalko @vincentqb
